Vectorize a Function

Source: R/vectorize.R
vectorize.Rd

Return a new function that maps f over an axis of its arguments: it applies f to every slice along that axis, by default the last, so to every column of a matrix. This is in the spirit of base::Vectorize(), but unlike it, vectorize() maps over slices, not elements. Instead of looping over the slices, the function is rewritten to operate on the whole batch at once.

This is analogous to vmap found in other array computing frameworks.

See the Vectorization article for more details.

Usage

vectorize(f, in_axes = -1L, out_axes = -1L, randomness = "independent")

Arguments

f

(function)
Function to vectorize.

in_axes

(integer(1) | named list())
Specify the batch axis. If in_axes is a single integer, it maps over that axis of every argument that is an array with at least one axis, an R array as well as an AnvlArray. Every application gets the other arguments as they are, such as a scalar, which has no axis to map over. If it is a named list, it must be compatible with the argument tree of the function. The values of the tree must either be integers, indicating the batch axis (negative values count from the end), or NULL, indicating no batching. Values are applied to all leaves of the node. Arguments or named elements the list leaves out are not batched either. Every argument that the list gives an axis must have it, so it cannot give one to a scalar.

out_axes

(integer(1) | list())
Along which axis to stack the outputs of f. Specified like in_axes, but a tree follows the structure of what f returns. NULL returns an output as it is, which only works for one that does not differ between the slices: it depends neither on the arguments mapped over nor, with randomness = "independent", on random numbers.

randomness

(character(1))
How the slices draw random numbers. With "independent" (the default), they draw independent random numbers: every slice draws the numbers a loop applying f to one slice after the other draws for it, and the random state advances as after that loop, so replacing such a loop with vectorize() gives the same results. With "common", they draw common random numbers: every slice draws those a single application of f draws, and the random state advances as after that application.

Value

(function)
Has the same formals as f and must be called inside jit(). It returns what f returns, with the batch axis added to every output where out_axes puts it; an output whose entry in out_axes is NULL is returned as it is.

Differences from base R

Unlike base::Vectorize() and the apply functions:

  • vectorize() maps over slices along an axis, not over elements: over the columns of a matrix by default, not over its numbers.

  • Arguments are not recycled, as elsewhere in anvl: every argument mapped over must have the same number of slices.

  • Results are not flattened: every output keeps the shape f gives it, with the batch axis added, where sapply() and apply() would turn a matrix result into a column.

  • A negative axis counts from the end: the default in_axes = -1L maps over the last axis, while x[-1] leaves out the first element.

See also

rule_vectorize(), gradient(), the Vectorization article

Examples

# f is written for a single vector
f <- function(x, y) sum(x * y)
x <- nv_array(matrix(1:6, nrow = 2L), dtype = "f32")
y <- nv_array(c(1, 2), dtype = "f32")

# one dot product per column of x, against the same y
jit(vectorize(f, in_axes = list(x = -1L)))(x, y)
#> AnvlArray
#>   5
#>  11
#>  17
#> [ CPUf32{3} ] 

# map over the rows instead: each row divided by its sum
jit(vectorize(function(x) x / sum(x), in_axes = 1L, out_axes = 1L))(x)
#> AnvlArray
#>  0.1111 0.3333 0.5556
#>  0.1667 0.3333 0.5000
#> [ CPUf32{2,3} ] 

# a nested list in in_axes maps over a part of a nested argument: the
# columns of params$w, while params$b is the same for every column
affine <- function(params, y) sum(params$w * y) + params$b
params <- list(w = x, b = nv_scalar(10, dtype = "f32"))
jit(vectorize(affine, in_axes = list(params = list(w = -1L))))(params, y)
#> AnvlArray
#>  15
#>  21
#>  27
#> [ CPUf32{3} ] 

# out_axes as a list: stack the dot products, and return the norm of y,
# which does not depend on the columns, as it is
dot_norm <- function(x, y) list(dot = sum(x * y), norm = sqrt(sum(y^2)))
jit(vectorize(
  dot_norm,
  in_axes = list(x = -1L),
  out_axes = list(dot = -1L, norm = NULL)
))(x, y)
#> $dot
#> AnvlArray
#>   5
#>  11
#>  17
#> [ CPUf32{3} ] 
#> 
#> $norm
#> AnvlArray
#>  2.2361
#> [ CPUf32{} ] 
#> 

# vectorize() composes with other transformations, e.g. one gradient of a
# loss per column of x
loss <- function(w, x) sum((x * w)^2)
jit(vectorize(gradient(loss, wrt = "w"), in_axes = list(x = -1L)))(y, x)
#> $w
#> AnvlArray
#>    2  18  50
#>   16  64 144
#> [ CPUf32{2,3} ] 
#> 

# and with itself: every column of x against every column of x, which is
# t(x) %*% x
f_all <- vectorize(vectorize(f, in_axes = list(x = -1L)), in_axes = list(y = -1L))
jit(f_all)(x, x)
#> AnvlArray
#>   5 11 17
#>  11 25 39
#>  17 39 61
#> [ CPUf32{3,3} ] 

# every column gets noise of its own, the noise a loop over the columns
# would draw
noisy <- function(x) x + nv_rnorm(shape = 2L)
nv_set_seed(1L)
jit(vectorize(noisy))(x)
#> AnvlArray
#>  1.8863 4.0593 5.4281
#>  0.7194 4.7140 7.4333
#> [ CPUf32{2,3} ] 
# or the same noise for every column
jit(vectorize(noisy, randomness = "common"))(x)
#> AnvlArray
#>  -0.7255  1.2745  3.2745
#>   2.4136  4.4136  6.4136
#> [ CPUf32{2,3} ]
